blocks.content: Some things in software should only exist once.
A logger. A config manager. A database connection pool. Create more than one of these and you get inconsistent behavior, wasted resources, and hard-to-trace bugs.
This is exactly what the Singleton Pattern solves.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773261-5d57476d.png
The idea is straightforward: a class that controls its own creation and guarantees only one instance ever exists no matter how many times you try to create it.
Simple to understand. Surprisingly tricky to implement correctly. Easy to misuse.
In this chapter we will cover what Singleton is, how it works, different ways to implement it, real-world examples, and the trade-offs you should know before using it.
1. What is the Singleton Pattern?
Singleton is a creational design pattern that guarantees a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
Two things define it:

["Single instance no matter how many times any part of your code asks for it, the same object comes back.","Global access any component can reach it directly without it being passed around through constructors or parameters."]
items: Single instance no matter how many times any part of your code asks for it, the same object comes back.
Global access any component can reach it directly without it being passed around through constructors or parameters.

blocks.content: Real-World Analogy

Think of a country's central bank. There is one. Every financial institution connects to the same one. If every bank created its own central bank, monetary policy would collapse into chaos. One instance coordinates everything.
Singleton works the same way.
Where It's Actually Used

["Loggers one logging object writes to one output stream consistently across the entire app.
","Database connection pools one pool manages and reuses connections so the system doesn't spin up hundreds of them.
","Cache objects one in-memory cache shared across the application so every component reads the same data.
","Thread pools one pool of worker threads shared system-wide to prevent resource overuse.
","Configuration managers one object holds app settings so every part of the system reads from the same source.
","App state one object tracks user session or application state so nothing falls out of sync.
"]
items: Loggers one logging object writes to one output stream consistently across the entire app.
Database connection pools one pool manages and reuses connections so the system doesn't spin up hundreds of them.
Cache objects one in-memory cache shared across the application so every component reads the same data.
Thread pools one pool of worker threads shared system-wide to prevent resource overuse.
Configuration managers one object holds app settings so every part of the system reads from the same source.
App state one object tracks user session or application state so nothing falls out of sync.

blocks.content: The pattern everywhere the same answer: one instance, shared by all, controlled by itself.
2. Class Diagram
For a class to behave as a Singleton, we need to take away the ability of outside code to freely create instances. The class itself must be the only one in charge of its own creation.
On top of that, there must be a controlled doorway through which the rest of the application can reach that single instance.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773356-718bd60d.png

["The instance field holds the one object that the entire application shares.","The private constructor makes it impossible for any outside code to create a fresh instance using new.","The getInstance() method is the only entry point call it from anywhere and you always get back the exact same object."]
items: The instance field holds the one object that the entire application shares.
The private constructor makes it impossible for any outside code to create a fresh instance using new.
The getInstance() method is the only entry point call it from anywhere and you always get back the exact same object.

blocks.content: Why not just use a global variable?
blocks.text: Why not just use a global variable?

blocks.content: On the surface, global variables seem to do the same job. But they only handle access they do nothing about creation. A Singleton goes further. It decides exactly when the object gets created, supports lazy initialization so the object only exists when it is first needed, handles thread safety during startup, and actively prevents duplicate instances from ever being born.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773584-1e2c5bc3.jpg
3. How It Works
The Singleton workflow is straightforward:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773696-53fc686a.png
Step 1: First Request A client calls Singleton.getInstance(). The method checks if an instance already exists.
Step 2: Instance Creation No instance exists yet so the method creates one using the private constructor and stores it in the static field.
Step 3: Return Instance The freshly created instance is returned to the caller.
Step 4: Subsequent Requests Every future call to getInstance() finds the instance already sitting in the static field and returns it immediately no creation, no overhead.
The sequence diagram shows two clients requesting the instance. The first triggers creation. The second gets the existing one back. Both end up pointing to the exact same object in memory.
4. Implementation

Singleton implementation varies across languages. The central challenge is thread safety: if two threads call getInstance()simultaneously when no instance exists yet, both might create separate instances breaking the entire guarantee.
We will start with the simplest approach and progressively improve it.
1. Lazy Initialization (Not Thread-Safe)
This approach creates the Singleton instance only when it is first needed saving resources if the Singleton is never actually used.
getInstance()checks if an instance already exists. If not, it creates and stores one. If it does, it simply returns the existing instance.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773799-931e76db.png

This implementation has a serious flaw. If two threads call getInstance() at the same time while instance is still null, both can pass the null check and create separate objects. This breaks the Singleton guarantee.
That’s why simple lazy initialization is not safe in a multi-threaded environment.
2. Thread-Safe Singleton

This approach extends lazy initialization by ensuring the Singleton is safe in multi-threaded environments. When multiple threads try to access the instance at the same time, synchronization ensures only one thread creates the object while others wait.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773917-3a59c6f2.png

The instance is created only when it is first requested. When a thread enters getInstance(), it acquires a lock, forcing other threads to wait. Once the lock is released, the waiting threads proceed and find that the instance has already been created. As a result, only one instance is ever created even under heavy concurrent access.

blocks.content: Performance Consideration
While this approach is correct and thread-safe, it has a performance drawback. Every call to getInstance() requires acquiring a lock, even after the instance has already been initialized.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245774037-71452869.png
3. Double-Checked Locking
Double-checked locking reduces performance overhead by only synchronizing during the first object creation. After the instance exists, threads skip the lock entirely.

["First check avoids locking when the instance already exists fast path for all subsequent calls.","Second check inside the lock catches the edge case where multiple threads passed the first check simultaneously.","The instance is only created when both checks confirm it does not exist yet."]
items: First check avoids locking when the instance already exists fast path for all subsequent calls.
Second check inside the lock catches the edge case where multiple threads passed the first check simultaneously.
The instance is only created when both checks confirm it does not exist yet.

blocks.content: Good Performance. Once the instance exists, threads hit the first check, see it is not null, and return immediately no locking, no waiting, no overhead.
4. Eager Initialization

In eager initialization, the Singleton instance is created as soon as the class is loaded before any thread can access it. That makes it inherently thread-safe without any explicit locks, because initialization happens exactly once during class loading.
This approach works well when your application always uses the Singleton, or when the cost of creating it is minimal.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245774165-d0b3ad37.png

Astatic finalfield stores the single shared instance. The instance is created when the class is loaded, not when it is first requested. No synchronization or locks are required because the JVM guarantees that static fields are initialized only once in a thread-safe manner.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245774329-51e38728.jpg

If the Singleton is lightweight and always needed eager initialization is the simplest and cleanest choice. If it is expensive to create or might never be used lazy initialization is the better option.
Singleton Implementations
Approach 1: Bill Pugh / Initialization-on-Demand Holder

This approach uses a static inner class to defer instance creation until getInstance() is first called. The JVM guarantees that inner classes are not loaded until they are referenced giving us lazy initialization without any synchronization.

Holder is not loaded when BillPughSingleton is loaded. It is only loaded when getInstance() is called for the first time triggering the initialization of INSTANCE. Class initialization in Java is guaranteed thread-safe by the JLS with no explicit synchronization needed.
The Bill Pugh approach delivers a perfect balance of lazy initialization, thread safety, and performance without the complexity of double-checked locking.
Approach 2: Enum Singleton (Recommended)
This is the simplest and safest approach in Java. Joshua Bloch recommends it in Effective Java as the best way to implement a Singleton.
The JVM provides four guarantees no other approach can match:

["Thread-safe initialization enum constants are initialized exactly once at class load time.","Serialization safety deserializing always returns the same instance, never a duplicate.","Reflection safety the JVM blocks creating enum instances via reflection entirely.","Single instance guaranteed enforced at the JVM level, not by your own code."]
items: Thread-safe initialization enum constants are initialized exactly once at class load time.
Serialization safety deserializing always returns the same instance, never a duplicate.
Reflection safety the JVM blocks creating enum instances via reflection entirely.
Single instance guaranteed enforced at the JVM level, not by your own code.

blocks.content: The only limitation enums cannot extend other classes. If your Singleton needs a base class, this approach won't work.
Approach 3: Static Block Initialization
Similar to eager initialization but uses a static initializer block. The key advantage is the ability to handle exceptions during instance creation gracefully.

["The static block executes once when the class is loaded by the JVM.","If an exception occurs during creation it is caught and wrapped cleanly in a RuntimeException.","Thread-safe but not lazy-loaded."]
items: The static block executes once when the class is loaded by the JVM.
If an exception occurs during creation it is caught and wrapped cleanly in a RuntimeException.
Thread-safe but not lazy-loaded.

blocks.content: Use this when the constructor might throw checked exceptions and you want to handle them gracefully during class loading rather than letting them propagate as unhandled errors. Thread-safe but not lazy-loaded which might be a drawback if initialization is resource-intensive or the Singleton is never actually used.
5. Practical Example: Application Logger
Imagine you are building an application where multiple components HTTP handlers, database layer, background jobs all need to log messages to the same output file.
You want one shared logger so that all log messages appear in order, in one place, without duplicate writes or conflicting file handles.

codes.python:
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum


class Logger(Enum):
    INSTANCE = "instance"

    def log(self, level, message):
        timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
        print(f"[{timestamp}] [{level}] {message}")

    def info(self, message):
        self.log("INFO", message)

    def warn(self, message):
        self.log("WARN", message)

    def error(self, message):
        self.log("ERROR", message)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Both references point to the same Logger instance
    logger1 = Logger.INSTANCE
    logger2 = Logger.INSTANCE

    print("Same instance?", logger1 is logger2)  # True

    # Different components logging through the same instance
    logger1.info("User:42 logged in successfully")
    logger2.warn("Payment retry attempt for Order:99")
    logger1.error("Database connection timeout")
    logger2.info("Background job completed")

blocks.content: Benefits Achieved:

• One shared logger no duplicate file handles or conflicting writes
  • Every component's log message appears in the same ordered output
  • Timestamp formatting handled in one place consistently
  • Thread-safe by design using Enum Singleton
  • No need to pass logger references through constructors or parameters
6. Pros and Cons of Singleton Pattern
blocks.text: 6. Pros and Cons of Singleton Pattern

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245774491-1093360a.jpg
Use Singleton judiciously. When loose coupling and testability matter and they usually do consider dependency injection as a cleaner alternative.
